I've been a loyal T-Mobile customer since 2016, when they launched the T-Mobile ONE plan. I've always received the military discount, but even with that discount, my monthly bill ballooned to $113 per month thanks to T-Mobile's price hikes. That was enough for me — I started looking for cheaper alternatives. Combined with Apple's iPhone 18 Pro costing at least $100 more this year, I figured if I was going to upgrade my phone anyway, the savings from a cheaper phone plan could help offset the cost. So I started looking into MVNOs.

What is an MVNO?

An MVNO is a "Mobile Virtual Network Operator." Simply put, MVNOs are wireless carriers that don't own their own nationwide cellular networks. They purchase network access from the major carriers — AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon — and resell the service to their own customers. Think of them as wireless resellers.

Switching to an MVNO doesn't necessarily mean giving up your current network. For example, Mint Mobile uses T-Mobile's network, Visible uses Verizon's, and US Mobile lets customers choose between all three major networks. In this article, I'll focus on these three MVNOs since they were the ones I researched most before leaving T-Mobile, but there are plenty of other options out there.

Ultimately, MVNOs offer you another way to buy cellular service besides going directly to the network owners.

Why Are MVNOs Cheaper, and What's the Catch?

If an MVNO uses the same network as AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon, how can it be so much cheaper? The short answer is that MVNOs don't shoulder all the costs of running a nationwide wireless operation. They don't build or maintain networks, many operate primarily online without physical retail stores, and they have fewer employees. Those savings can be passed on to customers in the form of lower monthly rates.

MVNO plans tend to be simpler, without many of the "perks" and extras that traditional carriers offer. Depending on the carrier and plan, you might not get free streaming services or other perks designed to keep you on a major network. But the money you save on an MVNO can easily offset the cost of subscribing to those "free" perks yourself if you want them.

That's been my experience. I loved T-Mobile's free MLB.TV subscription every year and took advantage of it every season. But I never watch Netflix, so the "Netflix on Us" perk was completely wasted on me. Even if I wanted Netflix and MLB.TV, I could subscribe to them myself and still come out ahead compared to what I save on my phone bill. At the end of the day, I just want reliable, reasonably priced cellular service — I don't need T-Mobile to throw in extras to keep me as a customer.

The "catch" isn't necessarily worse service — it's that you're buying less. What you actually give up depends on the MVNO and plan you choose. Video streaming may be limited to lower resolution, the amount of high-speed or premium data available may differ, and network priority may not be the same. With very fast Wi-Fi at home and rarely attending concerts or sporting events where networks get congested, network priority isn't a big concern for my everyday use. But since I sometimes travel internationally, international data is an important consideration. Some MVNOs include international data and texting, while others charge extra or offer limited coverage.

There are also some less obvious differences, especially when buying a new iPhone. If you use an MVNO, Apple Card Monthly Installments and the iPhone Upgrade Program aren't available. For those, you're limited to AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon. Practically speaking, this means if you buy your iPhone directly from Apple, you'll usually have to pay the full price upfront. The major carriers can also offer large trade-in credits or other incentives that generally aren't available with MVNOs. Apple Watch support isn't universal either, so if you have a cellular Apple Watch, that's worth keeping in mind.

Finally, most MVNOs primarily offer phone and live chat support rather than face-to-face help at physical stores. I'm reasonably tech-savvy and don't want to wait in line at a store for assistance anyway. In my experience, store reps just end up calling the same people you would, so waiting at home isn't really that different. This wasn't a deal-breaker for me.

Most importantly, none of these are absolute limits of MVNOs. Different carriers and plans vary, so it's worth understanding exactly what you're getting before you switch.

Three MVNOs Worth Considering

After I decided to leave T-Mobile, I started looking at my other options. Verizon and AT&T's postpaid plans were even more expensive than what I was already paying, so those two major carriers were immediately out. I narrowed my search to US Mobile, Mint Mobile, and Visible. Each had something appealing, and all three offered me a way to significantly cut my monthly wireless costs without giving up access to a major network.

US Mobile is probably the most flexible of the three and is ultimately the carrier I switched to from T-Mobile. That doesn't necessarily mean it's the best fit for you, or even the best of the three — it's just the one that suited my personal needs best.

Actually, US Mobile wasn't my first choice initially. I came across the company while researching MVNOs. But the more I looked at what they offered, the more they stood out. Here's why: US Mobile operates on all three major U.S. networks, letting customers choose whichever works best for them. They also offer an add-on called Multi-Network that lets you activate two networks on the same iPhone simultaneously, without needing a second phone number. Both networks are tied to the same line, and your iPhone will use whichever network has a stronger connection. So if T-Mobile's network works well at your office but Verizon's is stronger at home, you get the best of both without carrying two phones or managing two numbers. This feature costs extra from US Mobile and isn't something I personally need, but I thought it was a pretty unique option.

I recently moved and was curious how Verizon's coverage compared to T-Mobile's around my new home, so I decided to test both networks. I set my wife's iPhone to US Mobile's Light Speed network (T-Mobile) and put my iPhone on Warp (Verizon) so we could compare coverage ourselves. In our area, Verizon was clearly better, which made switching to US Mobile a win-win: stronger coverage and a much lower bill.

Mint Mobile was originally my top choice because it's a T-Mobile-owned brand, meaning I could keep using the same network I was familiar with at a much lower price. What I didn't like was that it doesn't include international data. My wife and I love taking cruises — international travel is part of our lifestyle — so having cellular data outside the U.S. is important to us. Mint does offer international data, but at an extra cost that quickly eats into the savings. I also didn't like that taxes and fees were charged on top.

Visible is equally straightforward, but it only uses Verizon's network. My biggest hesitation with Visible was Verizon's coverage in my area. I've been with T-Mobile for nearly a decade and know exactly how the network performs, but I had no idea about Verizon's coverage where I live. That was the only thing holding me back from choosing Visible over US Mobile, since US Mobile let me try Verizon's network and switch to T-Mobile or AT&T if it didn't work out. Visible's top-tier unlimited plan also includes a free cellular Apple Watch line, which was another attractive selling point. (US Mobile's top-tier plan on their Warp network, which is Verizon, offers the same perk.)

What You'll Need

Switching to an MVNO was even easier than I expected. My wife and I kept our existing iPhones and transferred both lines from T-Mobile to US Mobile in about ten minutes without even getting off the couch. You'll need an unlocked, compatible iPhone (or Android phone, though I'm focused on iPhone here), along with some information from your current carrier. If you want to keep your existing phone number, make sure you don't cancel your old service before the number has been ported over.

Here's what you need to switch:

  • Account number with your current wireless carrier
  • Transfer PIN
  • An unlocked, compatible iPhone
  • A new eSIM
  • A little patience

I prepaid US Mobile for two unlimited lines for the full year in preparation for the switch. My wife doesn't use a cellular Apple Watch and doesn't care about higher video resolution, so she opted for US Mobile's Unlimited Starter plan, saving $100 compared to my Unlimited Premium plan. Two lines plus an Apple Watch line came to $500 for the year, compared to the $1,356 per year I was paying T-Mobile for two lines with no Apple Watch service. That's a significant savings. (Again, this already includes the military discount!)

Getting the transfer PIN from T-Mobile was straightforward — I was half-expecting the process to be buried and complicated, but it wasn't. Here are instructions for Verizon and AT&T.

Once my iPhone was connected to Wi-Fi, US Mobile sent me a new eSIM, and the installation process was as simple as clicking a button in an email and following the on-screen prompts. My wife's iPhone was exactly the same. The only additional step was setting up my Apple Watch, which I did easily through the US Mobile app.

Why I'll Continue Using an MVNO

Same coverage, lower price: Based on what I'm saving, the trade-offs have been well worth it. With fast Wi-Fi at home, mobile data isn't a huge priority for me (though in speed tests, US Mobile was just as fast as T-Mobile). What matters most to me is having a strong, reliable cellular signal outside of Wi-Fi range, especially for calls and texts.

No long-term contracts: Most carriers have moved away from traditional contract plans, instead using device installment plans that effectively tie you to their network until the device is paid off. I've always bought my iPhones directly from Apple because I want the freedom of owning an unlocked device, but I also appreciate that US Mobile, Mint, and Visible don't require contracts.

Easy to switch: Most MVNOs bill monthly, so you're not locked into a long contract. If one carrier has a good deal this month and another has a better one next month, switching is quick and easy. Prepaid accounts also don't require a credit check, meaning each time a carrier runs a credit inquiry, your credit record won't take a hit — unlike with postpaid accounts, and you won't be denied because of poor credit. My credit is fine, but I didn't want a hard inquiry from switching from T-Mobile to Verizon to affect it.

Save more by prepaying: The trade-off for flexibility is that if you're willing to prepay for a year of service, you can save even more. Most MVNOs offer significant discounts for annual plans, so you're essentially trading the freedom to switch at any time for a lower overall price.

No surprise charges: As I mentioned earlier, my wife and I love taking cruises. If you've ever forgotten to put your iPhone in airplane mode after boarding and it connects to the ship's cellular network, you know the shocking bill that can follow. With a prepaid plan, I don't have to worry about accidentally racking up a massive roaming bill. If international roaming isn't included in the plan, my phone simply won't connect to foreign networks and charge me. US Mobile's plans also include all taxes and fees, so the listed price is exactly what you pay.

Switching to an MVNO isn't just about finding the cheapest service — it's about buying the service you actually want without paying for things you don't need. So far, I don't feel like I'm missing anything that matters to me (though I'll definitely miss that free MLB.TV subscription). In fact, I now have an Apple Watch line I didn't have before, and my monthly bill is lower. I'm using the same iPhone and the same phone number, and coverage in my area is actually better with US Mobile's Warp (Verizon) than before. And if I find a better option in the future, I'm free to switch again.

Your priorities may be different from mine, and MVNOs may not be right for everyone. But if you're currently paying a lot for wireless service and haven't considered an MVNO, it's worth looking into. You might be surprised at how little you actually have to give up.
